claims.claim: Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland in 2024. Where exactly it came from is still unknown
claims.source_checked: api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 (title, abstract, published online 2024-08-14); Clarke 2024 full text via the Firecrawl research index (pmcid:PMC11324516); api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (ABSTRACT ONLY); api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (ABSTRACT ONLY)
claims.note: Clarke 2024, title 'A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge', online 14 Aug 2024; body: the isotopic data 'indicate that the Altar Stone of Stonehenge has a provenance from the ORS in the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland'. Pirrie 2026 abstract: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown'. Clarke 2026 abstract: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. Caveat: Pirrie 2026 read as abstract only; the abstract does not say the stone is not Scottish, but if its full text argues against Scotland altogether, 'traced to Scotland' would need a qualifier.

claims.claim: In 2024, Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1: Crossref abstract and full text via the research index (pmcid:PMC11324516)
claims.note: A4: a viewer who swipes at second two hears only this, over a photo of Stonehenge. It is a true statement of what the 2024 paper did (abstract: detrital ages 'reveal a remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland'; body: 'indicate ... a provenance from the ORS in the Orcadian Basin'). 'Traced' matches the paper's own claim; neither 2026 abstract says it is wrong.

claims.claim: Exactly where it came from is still unknown.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090 and doi:10.1002/jqs.70080: ABSTRACTS ONLY (Crossref; lyellcollection.org and onlinelibrary.wiley.com return a Cloudflare challenge, 403; not in the research index); doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 full text (PDF, journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/3293/galley/18572/download/)
claims.note: Pirrie 2026 abstract: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown'. Clarke 2026 abstract: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. 'Still' holds: Parker Pearson 2024 p.129, 'As yet, the actual outcrop from which the Altar Stone was extracted is unknown'; Clarke 2024 named a basin, not an outcrop.

claims.source_checked: commons.wikimedia.org API for File:Sunrise_at_Stonehenge-_Red_sky_in_the_morning.jpg returned HTTP 429 (rate limited) twice; flickr.com/photos/stonehenge-stone-circle/11774816654 refused by the proxy (403). Viewed public/img/stonehenge-red-sky.jpg itself.

claims.claim: Stonehenge (approx.) pin at lon -1.826, lat 51.179
claims.source_checked: whc.unesco.org/en/list/373, historicengland.org.uk list entry 1010140, nominatim.openstreetmap.org, wikidata.org: all refused by the proxy (403). claims.claim: EXACT SOURCE / unknown, with a '?' over NE Scotland
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090 and doi:10.1002/jqs.70080 (ABSTRACTS ONLY, Crossref); doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 full text

claims.claim: The ages of tiny mineral grains inside it matched sandstone in the northeast.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 full text via research index (pmcid:PMC11324516)
claims.note: Clarke 2024 dated detrital zircon, apatite and rutile 'from two fragments of the Altar Stone'; heavy mineral grains 'typically 10–40 µm wide', target zircons 'usually <30 µm'. 'The detrital zircon age spectra from Orcadian Basin ORS provides the closest match to the Altar Stone detrital ages' (KS test cannot distinguish them), and apatite ages from Spittal, Caithness and Cruaday, Orkney 'match those from the Altar Stone'. Pirrie 2026 abstract agrees the grain dating 'supports a Laurentian source for the heavy minerals'.

claims.claim: THE ALTAR STONE / thin sections, dated grains (image public/img/altar-stone-thin-sections.jpg; camera closes on the zircon labelled 1,092 ± 18 Ma on 'tiny')
claims.where: on-screen: tag 'THE ALTAR STONE' and figure image
claims.source_checked: Viewed public/img/altar-stone-thin-sections.jpg; Clarke 2024 Fig. 2 caption and methods via research index (pmcid:PMC11324516); public/SOURCES.json entry. The original figure file could not be downloaded for a pixel comparison (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov serves a reCAPTCHA page; media.springernature.com and nature.com refused, 403).
claims.note: Fig. 2 caption: 'False colour automated mineralogy maps from thin sections of the Altar Stone ... U–Pb ablation pits ... shown with age (in millions of years ago, Ma), with uncertainty at the 2σ level.' The image shows sections labelled MS3 and 2010K.240 (the paper's two Altar Stone thin sections), a 1 mm scale bar, '24 µm U–Pb ablations' (methods: spot size ~24 µm), and dated grains: zircon 1,092 ± 18 Ma and 1,026 ± 25 Ma, apatite 462 ± 4 Ma, rutile 451 ± 8 Ma (the paper's Group 1 apatite and rutile lower intercepts are 462 ± 4 and 451 ± 8 Ma). No legend is present, consistent with 'cropped above the mineral legend'. Every detail agrees with Fig. 2; the label says no more than the caption.

claims.claim: If so, how did six tonnes travel more than seven hundred kilometres?

'More than seven hundred' sits under 'at least 750 km'; Clarke 2026 gives 'some 700 km'. 'If so' keeps the paper's condition ('Such a provenance implies').

claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 full text via research index

claims.claim: The 2024 team suggested it went by sea.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 (Crossref abstract; full text via research index)
claims.note: Abstract: 'The difficulty of long-distance overland transport of such massive cargo from Scotland, navigating topographic barriers, suggests that it was transported by sea.' Body: 'the geography of Britain and Ireland would have permitted sea routes southward from the Orcadian Basin towards southern England'. 'Suggested' matches 'suggests'.

claims.claim: BY SEA? / route not known; two dashed sea routes (EAST down the North Sea coast to off Selsey, WEST round the north and west coasts to Swanage)
claims.where: on-screen: tag 'BY SEA?' and map routes EAST/WEST
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 full text via research index; src/shorts/altar-stone/coast.json (every segment of EAST and WEST sampled at 401 points and tested point-in-polygon against all 101 rings)
claims.note: No sample point of either route falls on land. Closest approaches: EAST about 3 km off Flamborough Head; WEST about 5 km off the Mull of Oa (Islay) and ends about 0.7 km off the Purbeck shore at Swanage, i.e. at a landing, not inland. Clarke 2024 names no specific route, so 'route not known' with both coasts drawn is accurate.

claims.claim: A glacier? A 2026 ice model says ice could have carried it part of the way, at most.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1002/jqs.70080: ABSTRACT ONLY (api.crossref.org; online 2026-06-04; Wiley full text behind a Cloudflare challenge, 403; not in the research index)
claims.note: Abstract: 'we combine sandstone provenance analysis with ice flow modelling'; 'Glacial dispersal to Dogger Bank would reduce the anthropogenic transport distance required to Stonehenge from 700 km to 400 km'; 'Glacial transport may have provided an intermediate stage in the stone's journey, but alone cannot account for the final emplacement on Salisbury Plain. Even under a glacially assisted scenario, substantial anthropogenic transport would have remained necessary.' 'Could have ... part of the way, at most' fits 'may have provided an intermediate stage ... alone cannot account'. The abstract also raises a timing problem (Dogger Bank flooded before the stone likely arrived) that the script omits; the omission only leaves the glacier idea weaker than it is, not stronger than the source.

claims.claim: ICE MODEL / part of the way, at most
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1002/jqs.70080: ABSTRACT ONLY
claims.note: As claim 24.

claims.claim: Ice sheet outline, ice path from NE Scotland south-east to Dogger Bank, dashed human path from Dogger Bank to Stonehenge; 'ice extent and path illustrative'
claims.where: on-screen: map drawings ICE, ICE_PATH, PEOPLE_PATH and note
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1002/jqs.70080: ABSTRACT ONLY
claims.note: Abstract: from Caithness modelled glacial transport is 'predominantly towards the north-east, with a localised south-eastward pathway directed towards Dogger Bank', then 'substantial anthropogenic transport'. The drawn path follows that south-eastward pathway and the human leg; the outline and path are labelled illustrative on screen (A6). The human leg crosses present-day sea off Lincolnshire before reaching land; the abstract specifies no human route, and the recap labels routes illustrative.

claims.claim: Dogger Bank (approx.) pin at lon 1.2, lat 54.3
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1002/jqs.70080 ABSTRACT ONLY (no coordinates); marineregions.org and data.jncc.gov.uk refused by the proxy (403); Habibi Motlagh et al. 2025, doi:10.1016/j.dib.2025.111931 (pmcid:PMC12351168) via research index, Table 1 station coordinates
claims.note: The pin is 402 km great-circle from the Stonehenge pin, matching Clarke 2026's '400 km'. But no opened source puts the pin on Dogger Bank: the 2024 Senckenberg Dogger Bank monitoring stations all lie at about 54.47–55.66 N, 1.3–4.0 E, and the most south-westerly (DOG24:04, about 54.48 N, 1.86 E) is roughly 45 km east-north-east of the pin, which sits about 86 km off the Yorkshire coast. The pin may be on the bank's south-west margin or just off it. Fix: check the bank's outline against a citable boundary (e.g. JNCC Dogger Bank SAC or Marine Regions) and, if needed, move the pin onto it (e.g. near 54.5 N, 1.8 E, about 440 km from Stonehenge, still 'approx.' for the abstract's 400 km), or cite the source that shows 1.2 E, 54.3 N on the bank.
